stories.extended_summary: A whimsical sight awaited subway riders wandering the downtown B, D, F and M train platform at the West Fourth Street station on Saturday afternoon: a newly reopened newspaper kiosk with nothing for sale. stories.extended_summary: YUMA, Ariz. (KYMA) - Bubba's 33 brought the Yuma community together for its "Raise from the Roof" fundraiser, an event designed to support injured Veterans. The goal was to raise $5,000 while raising awareness for those who have sacrificed in service to our country. As part of the event, David Lopez, the restaurant's manager, climbed onto the roof and remained there until the goal was reached. Despite the extreme summer temperatures, he stayed on the roof for several hours. "The purpose is to make awareness and raise money, to cover as much as possible the bills of injured Veterans," Lopez shared. Throughout the day, several members of the community even climbed onto the roof to stand alongside Lopez. Jump to comments ↓

stories.title: Chelsea Firefighters Assist with Delivery of Baby Girl Inside CANA Tunnels in Charlestown
stories.summary: When gridlock trapped expectant parents in the CANA Tunnels, Chelsea firefighters rushed to the scene just as the mother gave birth. They helped deliver a healthy baby girl, clearing her airway and caring for the family until EMS arrived. The crew's quick thinking turned a stressful commute into a memorable arrival.
stories.extended_summary: It was 7 a.m. on Tuesday when Chelsea's Engine 4 got the call: a woman in labor, trapped in gridlock inside Boston's CANA Tunnels. By the time Lieutenant David Asci and firefighters Kevin Gomes and Santos Hernandez reached the car, the baby was already arriving. The crew immediately assessed the newborn, cleared her airway, clamped and cut the umbilical cord, and kept both mother and daughter stable until EMS took over. Chief John Quatieri called it "a truly special experience" and congratulated the parents on their healthy baby girl. It's a delivery story they'll never forget.

stories.title: Chicago’s Tiniest Bakery Is Attached To A Tree In Bucktown — And Full Of Free Cookies
stories.summary: Liz Tierney turned a tree in her Chicago neighborhood into a tiny bakery, filling a wooden box with free homemade cookies every weekend. The whimsical 'bakehouse' has become a beloved local treat, with around 100 cookies vanishing in a few hours. It's a small, sweet way to bring neighbors joy.
stories.extended_summary: It looks like a Little Free Library — but instead of books, it's stocked with cookies. Liz Tierney, a home baker inspired by her grandmother, installed the miniature bakehouse on a catalpa tree in Bucktown and now fills it with rotating flavors like sprinkle, chocolate chip, and pecan-toffee-oat. Neighbors can grab one free cookie on Saturdays and Sundays, and they regularly run out within hours. "My hope was people would be charmed by it," Tierney says. With cookies as the currency, that block just became a little more joyful.

stories.title: Christmas in July for Wilson’s Pool Room
stories.summary: After a fire destroyed Wilson's Pool Room and displaced families, Greg Dotson organized a 'Christmas in July' fundraiser that raised over $33,000 in one week for the Wilson family. Santa even made a special appearance in Versailles for the drawing. The community's generosity turned a tragedy into a lifeline.
stories.extended_summary: When a July 9 fire tore through Wilson's Pool Room, leaving the Wilson family and apartment tenants in need, Greg Dotson didn't wait for the holidays. He hosted a Christmas in July raffle — complete with a surprise visit from Santa — and in just seven days raised $33,590 to help the family rebuild. The event benefited the Wilsons and other displaced neighbors, showing how fast a community can rally. For the Wilsons, it might as well have been Christmas morning.

stories.title: College expands clubs to coast
stories.summary: At 85, David Glaubinger is launching a monthly writing group in Point Reyes Station, part of a college program expanding to the coast. Participants write for 15 minutes and share, with prompts drawn from local police logs. It's a simple invitation to tell stories and connect.
stories.extended_summary: The first rule: write for 15 minutes, anything, then share. That's the approach 85-year-old David Glaubinger brought to the inaugural meeting of a new writing group in Point Reyes Station, part of a college's effort to extend its clubs to the coast. For those stuck, prompts from the sheriff's calls offer plenty of material. The monthly gathering debuted in July, proving that a blank page and a group of neighbors are all it takes to spark creativity. At 85, Glaubinger is still leading by example.

stories.title: Combating isolation with entertainment
stories.summary: Andy MacDougall is fighting senior loneliness one vintage film at a time. He hosts weekly movie nights using 16mm projectors, bringing older adults together for a nostalgic escape and a sense of community. Science says meaningful connection is vital — Andy's making it fun.
stories.extended_summary: For decades, Andy MacDougall has hosted old-fashioned movie nights using 16mm projectors — the kind that click and flicker. His screenings at home and other venues give seniors (and anyone else) a regular social activity that combats isolation, which researchers warn can lead to heart disease and depression. The nostalgic hobby brings people together, giving them something to look forward to every week. It's proof that a reel of film can also wind up a community.

stories.title: Comment on Branching Out by Insulation Abm
stories.summary: The Blue Crew, part of the Northwest Youth Corps, spent the summer maintaining trees, reducing fire risk, and restoring habitats in Eugene. Eight teens, including 15-year-old Grafton Dietz, are gaining hands-on science experience while keeping the city green. It's a win for the youth and the environment.
stories.extended_summary: On a summer morning, the Blue Crew sets down their hard hats for a break. These eight teens, part of the Northwest Youth Corps, are among nearly 1,000 young people working to restore urban forests. They've cleared debris from flooded easements, spread mulch around neighborhood trees, and learned how science applies in the real world. "These trees are gonna last for many years," says 15-year-old Grafton Dietz. The program, funded by a federal grant, teaches leadership and gives parks the care they need — a transformation for both the crew and their community.

stories.title: Comment on Orphaned loon chick successfully fostered with new family by Ruth Gais
stories.summary: A loon chick, orphaned after being pecked by its sibling, was rescued from an Adirondack pond and successfully fostered into a new loon family. Wildlife experts from the Bronx Zoo and a local vet coordinated the delicate operation. The little loonlet gets a second chance.
stories.extended_summary: Less than a week old and alone, a tiny loon chick was found beached on Fish Creek Pond after losing a fight with its older sibling. Ken Huth and Hannah Hughes from the Bronx Zoo, in the area to band loons, tried reuniting it with its family — but the other chick attacked again. So they brought it to Dr. Nina Schoch, who cared for it and arranged fostering with a new loon family. Sibling rivalry is rare, but this rescue ensures the chick will grow up with a family after all.

stories.title: Comment on ‘A miracle took place’: Constantine policeman recognized for helping save woman’s life by Mister Hyde
stories.summary: After a woman stopped breathing on Easter Sunday, Sgt. Adam Stark performed CPR and used an AED until paramedics arrived. A third shock restarted her heart, and Emily Langston is now recovering at home. The officer was recognized at a village council meeting.
stories.extended_summary: Emily Langston was still in her car at church on Easter morning when she lost consciousness and stopped breathing. Sgt. Adam Stark arrived to find no pulse and immediately began CPR. Two shocks from an AED failed, but after a third, her heart began beating again. Paramedics took over and got her breathing, leading to her eventual recovery. At a recent council meeting, Stark was honored for his role — and Langston's family are among those calling it a miracle.

stories.title: Community groups collaborate to provide school supplies to hundreds of families
stories.summary: Fatherhood United and Laced Up 815 held their third annual back-to-school giveaway at The Sports Factory in Rockford, providing backpacks, shoes, haircuts, and supplies to about 1,200 students. Families lined up while supplies lasted, and no kid left empty-handed.
stories.extended_summary: At The Sports Factory, a line of families stretched out as volunteers handed out backpacks, shoes, and school supplies. Roughly 1,200 students received what they needed for the upcoming school year — plus fresh haircuts. The event, a partnership between Fatherhood United and Laced Up 815, has become an annual rite of summer in Rockford. With so many families struggling, this one-day boost ensures kids start the year ready to learn. And they did it all before the bell rang.

stories.title: Convicted felons at San Quentin pledge to become ambassadors of peace
stories.summary: At San Quentin, graduates of the Guiding Rage Into Power program pledged to become ambassadors of peace after completing a curriculum focused on mindfulness, emotional intelligence, and understanding victims. Their ceremony featured meditation and personal stories of change. It's a powerful step toward rehabilitation.
stories.extended_summary: In a ceremony at San Quentin, residents of the GRIP program took a deep breath together — one hand on heart, one on stomach — to mark their graduation. The program, which teaches mindfulness, emotional intelligence, and non-violence, has a waiting list so competitive the warden joked about it. Graduate Latice Collins spoke of the challenges her tribe faced, and each graduate pledged to spread peace. Their families watched as these men, who once made choices that led to prison, chose connection over correction.

stories.extended_summary: By Kai Curry NORTHWEST ASIAN WEEKLY Jet Lai (Photo provided by the Lai Family) Like most kids, 10-year-old Jet Lai has some trouble finishing his chores. Unlike most kids, Lai turned this into an opportunity. The inventive Whidbey Islander created an app that will tell parents when their kids really finish their chores. Called “ChoreCheck,” this app uses current digital technology to determine whether tasks get done, and limits screen time until they do. Lai made it to the quarter finals of Bill Nye’s America’s Favorite Student with his digital skills, which are what led him to creating the app shortly afterward. Lai now fears he won’t make it through any other contests, because, as he says, only half-jokingly, “I’ll probably be America’s most hated student after this app gets published.”
